source: Shaikh et al. (2024) Grounding Gaps in Language Model Generations
finding: LLMs given the same dialogue context as humans produce far fewer grounding acts (clarification, acknowledgment, follow-up). They tend to presume common ground instead of building it.
numbers: Off-the-shelf LLM turns are on average 77.5% less likely than human turns to contain grounding acts. Datasets include ESConv (mental-health support), simulated turn-taking.
limits: Task-oriented datasets; grounding acts detected by prompted few-shot classifiers, author-validated on a 10% test set.
agent_relevance: Our agent should not assume the user's intent is shared. It needs an explicit clarify step, written in code, not left to the model's habit.

source: Shaikh et al. (2024) Grounding Gaps in Language Model Generations
finding: Agreement between human and model on when to use a grounding act is poor, even when base rates match. Human-human agreement is much higher.
numbers: Human-LM Cohen kappa below 0.2 for most OpenAI variants; human-human kappa on ESConv averaged 37.5 (as printed, scale x100). Exception: gpt-3.5-instruct for follow-ups, 29.5 vs human 27.9 base rate, fair agreement.
limits: One dataset for the human-human check.
agent_relevance: Matching how often a behaviour occurs is not the same as using it at the right moment. Test timing, not just frequency.

source: Shaikh et al. (2024) Grounding Gaps in Language Model Generations
finding: Preference tuning lowers grounding. More DPO steps give lower agreement with humans. Preferred training answers contain fewer grounding acts.
numbers: After PPO the base rate fell about 7.0% across acts and kappa fell 39.0%; DPO gave a 42.5% kappa drop (Archangel models). No link for SFT steps (p>0.1). Chi-square 484.08, p<0.00001 for grounding being rarer in preferred examples.
limits: Open models only for this ablation; causal reading is partly inferential.
agent_relevance: Helpful-assistant tuning works against clarifying. A scaffold must counter it from outside the model.

source: Shaikh et al. (2024) Grounding Gaps in Language Model Generations
finding: A prompt telling the model to ground raised grounding but overshot, and did not fix timing. Authors call the gap hard to fix by prompting alone.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo with mitigation prompt: follow-ups 10.76 to 42.32, acknowledgment 1.05 to 2.54, clarification 0 to 1.16; clarification kappa went from 0 to -1.65 (worse than chance).
limits: One model and one prompt tested.
agent_relevance: A blanket 'ask questions' prompt is not enough. Trigger clarification by a code-checked ambiguity test.

source: Li et al. (2023) Theory of Mind for Multi-Agent Collaboration via Large Language Models
finding: In a text bomb-defusal team game, GPT-4 teams reached full score zero-shot. ChatGPT teams failed. Emergent leadership, helping and information sharing appeared.
numbers: ChatGPT team score averaged 43.3 and never completed the task. GPT-4 teams reached full score; with explicit belief state 12.3 rounds vs 28.3 (order as printed in text, check source). Baselines: CBS planner 6.0 rounds, MAPPO 11.0 after 45M steps.
limits: Small text game.
agent_relevance: Capable models do form common ground in a small closed world. Weak models do not.

source: Li et al. (2023) Theory of Mind for Multi-Agent Collaboration via Large Language Models
finding: ToM probe questions: accuracy falls with order for ChatGPT. Writing the belief state down helped GPT-4.
numbers: Introspection / 1st-order / 2nd-order accuracy: ChatGPT 79.0 / 41.9 / 11.6; GPT-4 80.0 / 60.0 / 64.3; GPT-4 + belief state 97.2 / 80.1 / 69.4.
limits: Answers annotated by experimenters; one game.
agent_relevance: An explicit written belief-about-partner state is a cheap scaffold with a measured gain. Fits our state-table idea.

source: Li et al. (2023) Theory of Mind for Multi-Agent Collaboration via Large Language Models
finding: Systematic failures: long-horizon context loss (invalid moves although rules were in the prompt) and hallucination about task state.
numbers: Examples in section 6.4; explicit belief representation mitigated them.
limits: Qualitative; counts only for the ToM table.
agent_relevance: Put key rules next to the question, or restate them each step. Do not rely on early prompt text.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Building Cooperative Embodied Agents Modularly with LLMs (CoELA)
finding: A modular LLM agent (perception, memory, communication, planning, execution) cooperates better than planner baselines, and humans trust it more when it talks in natural language.
numbers: C-WAH steps, symbolic obs: MHP+MHP 75 (33% gain), MHP+CoELA 59 (45%), CoELA+CoELA 57 (49%). TDW-MAT transport rate total 0.43 alone, 0.61 RHP+RHP, 0.69 RHP+CoELA, 0.71 CoELA+CoELA. Claims over 40% efficiency gain.
limits: CoELA run once per condition on C-WAH for cost; GPT-4 driven; LLAMA-2 only 0.53 until fine-tuned (CoLLAMA 0.70).
agent_relevance: Splitting memory, message-writing and planning into separate slots matches our program-decides design.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Building Cooperative Embodied Agents Modularly with LLMs (CoELA)
finding: Human user study: agents that talk are trusted more. Removing communication cut trust and efficiency.
numbers: Trust on 7-point scale: 6.3 for CoELA vs 4.7 without communication, t-test p=0.0003.
limits: Human sample size not recorded here; task-specific.
agent_relevance: Visible status messages build trust; our agent should report its current understanding.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) ProAgent: Building Proactive Cooperative Agents with LLMs
finding: An LLM agent that infers the teammate's intention and corrects that belief from observed behaviour beats self-play, PBT, FCP, MEP and COLE agents in Overcooked-AI.
numbers: Average improvement over 10% with human proxy partners vs the best prior method; 36 algorithm pairs, 5 episodes each, 5 layouts. Without the Verificator module success fell to 20% over 100 steps.
limits: Human proxies are behaviour-cloned models, not real people. One kitchen game.
agent_relevance: A belief-correction loop (predict partner, compare with what they did, update) is a transferable operator for user modelling.

source: Agashe et al. (2025) LLM-Coordination: Evaluating and Analyzing Multi-agent Coordination Abilities in LLMs
finding: LLM agents do well when coordination depends on world state (Overcooked) and badly when they must model partner beliefs (Hanabi). ToM and verification steps add measurable score.
numbers: Hanabi mean score: BAD 23.92, SAD 24.01, OBL 24.10 (RL); GPT-4-turbo 13.33; without ToM step 10.33; without ToM and verification 4.33; GPT-4o 8.33; GPT-3.5-turbo 1.33; Mixtral-8x7b 0.33. CoordQA has 198 multiple-choice items.
limits: Few games per model; scaffold designed by the authors.
agent_relevance: A verify-before-act step cut fatal plays. Supports our check operators.

source: Agashe et al. (2025) LLM-Coordination
finding: Environment comprehension correlates strongly with Overcooked success, ToM reasoning only moderately. In Hanabi both matter strongly.
numbers: Component scores for the four LLMs include EC 0.88/0.95/0.78/0.92, ToM 0.66/0.85/0.57/0.72, JP 0.85/0.98/0.68/0.89 (column-to-model mapping not verified).
limits: Correlation over only four models.
agent_relevance: Separate state-tracking skill from partner-modelling skill when testing our agent.

source: Ullman (2023) Large Language Models Fail on Trivial Alterations to Theory-of-Mind Tasks
finding: Small changes that keep the ToM logic (a transparent bag, an informed protagonist) flip GPT-3.5 answers. The earlier apparent success was not robust.
numbers: Kosinski's original: content prompt P(popcorn)=100%; belief prompts 0% popcorn / 99% chocolate. In the transparent-bag variant a model still put 95% on chocolate for a person who could see inside (as read).
quote: outlying failure cases should outweigh average success rates
limits: GPT-3.5 only; one task family.
agent_relevance: Evaluate our agent on perturbed variants, not only the standard probe.

source: He et al. (2023) Hi-ToM: A Benchmark for Evaluating Higher-Order Theory of Mind Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Accuracy drops as belief nesting goes up (0th to 4th) and when deceptive communication is added. Chain-of-thought prompting gave small, uneven gains.
numbers: Standard accuracy under vanilla prompt / CoT prompt: GPT-4 58.11 / 59.88; GPT-3.5-turbo 27.50 / 35.50 (+8.00); another chat model 46.33 on CoT. All below 60%.
limits: Scripted stories; multiple choice; per-order figures only seen in heatmaps.
agent_relevance: Do not expect reliable belief tracking beyond about second level. Use external notes for deeper nesting.

source: Kim et al. (2023) FANTOM: A Benchmark for Stress-testing Machine Theory of Mind in Interactions
finding: In multi-party conversations where someone leaves and returns, models fail to track who knows what, and answer from the full view rather than the person's limited view.
numbers: Human 87.5 on belief-choice; GPT-4 0613 + CoT 26.6 (June) / 14.8 (Oct); ChatGPT 0613 + CoT 3.7; Llama-2 Chat + CoT 0.4; Flan-T5 XL fine-tuned 53.7. Answerability and info-access: human 90.6; GPT-4 + CoT 40.2 / 57.7 (June).
limits: Scripts generated by an LLM; strict score needs every linked question right.
agent_relevance: Information asymmetry in conversation is where models break. Keep per-party knowledge tables in code.

source: Shi et al. (2025) MuMA-ToM: Multi-modal Multi-agent Theory of Mind
finding: On video-and-text questions about one person's belief about another's goal, humans are near ceiling while multimodal models sit near 50%.
numbers: Human overall 93.5; best large multimodal model Gemini 1.5 Pro 56.4; Llava 1.6 34B 52.8; GPT-4o 50.6 (column reading of a garbled table).
limits: Table text partly garbled in extraction; the paper's own inverse-planning method number not re-read.
agent_relevance: Higher-order social inference still needs explicit structured models, not plain prompting.

source: Cross et al. (2025) Hypothetical Minds: Scaffolding Theory of Mind for Multi-Agent Tasks with LLMs
finding: A ToM module writes hypotheses about the other agent's strategy, scores each by how well it predicts behaviour, and refines it. It beats LLM-agent and RL baselines on Melting Pot.
numbers: 30 distinct evaluation scenarios; authors report it outperforms baselines in every environment and most scenarios. Ablations show hypothesis evaluation and refinement matter.
limits: Exact per-scenario numbers not recorded; Melting Pot is simulated.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis, score, refine over a partner model is a concrete scaffold, close to our hypothesise-and-test operators.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
finding: Taxonomy of 14 failure modes in 3 groups from 1600+ annotated traces in 7 frameworks. Inter-agent misalignment includes failing to ask for clarification and ignoring others' input.
numbers: Failure rates 41% to 86.7% across 7 systems. FM-2.2 (wrong assumptions instead of clarifying) 6.80%, FM-2.3 task derailment 7.40%, FM-2.5 ignoring other agents 1.90%, FM-2.6 reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%. Kappa 0.88; LLM annotator accuracy 94%.
limits: Percentages are shares of annotated failures; traces mostly coding, math, agent tasks.
agent_relevance: The breakdown common-ground theory predicts shows up in agent teams. Log these modes in our own traces.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) MAST
finding: Fixing roles and workflow raised success without changing the model. Better messaging protocols (MCP, A2A) were judged insufficient for misalignment errors.
numbers: Improved role specification alone: +9.4% success for ChatDev with GPT-4o. The same figure is reported for making the CEO agent final decider.
limits: One system tested for the intervention.
agent_relevance: Structure, not extra chat, fixes team failures. Supports one agent with fixed states.

source: Shao et al. (2026) Collaborative Gym: A Framework for Enabling and Evaluating Human-Agent Collaboration
finding: Human-agent teams beat fully autonomous agents, yet communication and situational awareness failures remain common.
numbers: Win rate of best collaborative agent vs autonomous: 86% Travel Planning, 74% Tabular Analysis, 66% Related Work (real users). Communication failures in 65% and situational awareness failures in 40% of real cases (80% and 47% simulated; Spearman 0.803 between conditions).
limits: Failure categories overlap.
agent_relevance: Gains from joint work are real but the agent loses track of what the human is doing. Needs a shared-state view.

source: Shao et al. (2026) Collaborative Gym
finding: Non-turn-taking interaction (agent keeps working, human steps in any time) beat strict turn-taking with the same agent.
numbers: Travel planning: performance 0.84 vs 0.81, satisfaction 3.95 vs 3.55 (p=0.012), 70% preference win rate. Users spent 21-32% of actions controlling the environment directly.
limits: One agent (gpt-4o) in the ablation.
agent_relevance: Teammate-like behaviour is concurrent and interruptible. Interface point, background only.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: When the task is revealed in pieces over turns, all tested LLMs lose performance. They make early assumptions, answer prematurely, and do not recover.
numbers: Average 39% drop across six generation tasks over 200,000+ simulated conversations; unreliability up 112%; aptitude loss minor. Drop appears even with two turns.
limits: Simulated users revealing sharded instructions, not real people.
agent_relevance: Early wrong assumptions stick. Our agent should hold the answer back until the spec is complete.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: Repeating earlier user information (recap) helps only part way. Snowball (repeat all shards every turn) helps less than a final recap, and neither reaches the single-turn score.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini: sharded 50.4, recap 66.5, snowball 61.8, full 86.8; GPT-4o: sharded 59.1, recap 76.6, snowball 65.3, full 93.0 (column order inferred from table layout).
limits: Recap is unrealistic, since the last turn is unknown in advance.
agent_relevance: A code-run restatement of everything agreed so far is a measured partial fix.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems
finding: Multi-agent coordination helps on decomposable tasks and hurts on sequential or tool-heavy ones. Without a central check, errors multiply.
numbers: 260 configurations, 6 benchmarks, 5 architectures, 3 model families. Change vs single agent from +80.8% (financial reasoning) to -70.0% (sequential planning). Independent agents amplify errors 17.2x, centralized 4.4x. Single-agent baseline above 45% gives negative returns from more agents (beta -0.236). Predicts best architecture for 87% of held-out cases.
limits: Cross-validated R2 only 0.373.
agent_relevance: Supports staying single-agent plus a central verifier.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop Overvaluing Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Five multi-agent debate methods often fail to beat chain-of-thought or self-consistency, even at much higher compute. Mixing different models helps.
numbers: 5 methods, 9 benchmarks, 4 foundation models.
limits: Abstract level read; per-method numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: Debate between copies of one model adds little shared understanding. Avoid debate loops.

source: Han and Zhang (2025) Exploring Advanced LLM Multi-Agent Systems Based on Blackboard Architecture
finding: A classic AI shared-workspace design (blackboard) used for LLM agents: all agents read and write one board, a controller picks who acts, repeat until consensus.
numbers: Beats CoT methods by 4.33% on average and static multi-agent methods by 5.02%. Consensus by all agents on 89.8% of MMLU, 52.5% of GPQA, 29.4% of MATH items.
limits: Six benchmarks; MMLU subsampled to 20 per category.
agent_relevance: The blackboard is the machine version of a common-ground store. Our state table with code control resembles it.

source: Khebour et al. (2024) Common Ground Tracking in Multimodal Dialogue
finding: A pipeline extracts utterances, gestures and actions to track what a team has agreed on (accepted facts, open questions) in a block-weighing task.
numbers: Move classifier weighted F1 0.61; action annotation F1 0.67 (kappa 0.59); common ground annotation F1 0.54; semantic SMATCH F1 0.75.
limits: Modular older-style system on a small lab corpus; accuracy modest.
agent_relevance: Common ground as an explicit structure updated by accept and reject moves. Template for our shared-facts list.

source: Hu et al. (2020) Other-Play for Zero-Shot Coordination
finding: Self-play agents form private conventions that fail with new partners. Training under symmetry gives more human-compatible conventions.
numbers: Human study, 20 board-game-club players: with other-play bot 15.75 (s.e.m. 1.23), 45% bombed out; with self-play bot 9.15 (s.e.m. 1.18), 85% bombed out. Self-play bot scored 23.99 with itself, 20.99 across seeds.
limits: Hanabi only; small human sample.
agent_relevance: Private conventions are the machine form of lacking common ground. Use plain, explainable moves with others.

source: Guo et al. (2024) LLM based Multi-Agents: A Survey of Progress and Challenges
finding: Survey of LLM multi-agent systems covering communication structure, roles and collaboration paradigms.
numbers: No numbers recorded; only the first page was read.
limits: Title and abstract level only.
agent_relevance: Background map of the field.

source: Wu et al. (2025) CollabLLM: From Passive Responders to Active Collaborators
finding: Training with multi-turn-aware rewards makes the model ask and uncover user intent. Against baselines it improves task score and interactivity.
numbers: Averages: 18.5% higher task performance, 46.3% higher interactivity, 13.3% more efficient conversations; user study 17.6% higher satisfaction and 10.4% less user time.
limits: RL fine-tuning, outside our scaffold-only rule; mostly simulated users.
agent_relevance: Shows clarification can be rewarded and measured; a target for a code-run check.
